feedback: If a learner extends row by row to reach x=10, prompt them to use the ×3 multiplier directly: 10×3=30.
If a learner writes the fraction using the total as denominator (e.g. 2/8 for x:y=2:6), separate the readings: the ratio compares x to y (x is 1/3 of y); part-to-whole would compare x to x+y=8.
Confirm a double number line only shows equal ratios when both lines start at aligned zeros.
activities.intendedInsight: A ratio table encodes both a scalar multiplier (down columns) and a functional multiplier (across, the y=kx rule); the multiple can be used directly to predict any value. A double number line aligned at zero shows equal ratios lining up. Part-to-part and part-to-whole are different comparisons.
learnerActions: Take a ratio table and read DOWN the columns to find the scalar multiplier (how each row scales from the previous).
Read ACROSS the rows to find the constant functional relationship a:b / the y=kx rule between the two quantities.
Use a double number line aligned at 0 so that equal ratios line up, and check that both lines start at aligned zeros.
Given x=10 for a 1:3 relationship, work out y directly using the multiplier (×3) rather than extending the table row by row.

Distinguish 'x is 1/3 OF y' (part-to-part, the correct multiplicative reading) from 'x is a fraction of the whole x+y' (part-to-whole); for example, with 2 red : 5 blue beads, red is 2/5 of the blue count (part-to-part) but 2 out of 7 total beads (part-to-whole), anchoring each reading to its own picture.
activities.title: Read the ratio table both ways

feedback: For the x=2,y=5 / x=4,y=7 table, if a learner calls it a ratio, have them compute 5÷2=2.5 and 7÷4=1.75: the multiple is not constant, so it is additive (+3), not a ratio.
If a learner picks any straight line as proportional, ask where it crosses the y-axis: only a line through (0,0) represents y=kx.
When a learner matches 1:3 to y=3x, ask them to confirm the gradient of the line equals the multiple (3).
activities.intendedInsight: Sorting and matching across forms, with deliberate additive distractors, can check whether a learner can translate among ratio, fraction and linear form and can reject an additive table as not proportional. A straight-line graph only shows proportionality when it passes through the origin.
learnerActions: Sort several tables of values into 'ratio relationship' vs 'not a ratio relationship', justifying each by whether y÷x is constant.
Match equivalent forms: connect 1:3 with y=3x and with a straight line through the origin.
Predict y for a new x in a given table, with an additive answer offered as a tempting but wrong option, and explain why the additive choice fails.
Given two graphs, identify which shows proportionality and explain that it must pass through the origin.
Test a tricky table — x=2,y=5 and x=4,y=7 — and decide whether it is a ratio relationship (it is additive: +3 each time, but 5÷2 ≠ 7÷4, so no constant multiple).
activities.title: Sort and match: is it a ratio relationship?

feedback: If the learner reasons 'more red so darker' or 'different amounts so different', treat this as additive/absolute-amount reasoning and have them predict then check against y÷x.
Accept a full explanation only when it names the constant multiple AND notes that the difference is not constant.
Use the predict-observe-explain paint task so the reason stated before mixing is the diagnostic part.
activities.intendedInsight: Being pressed to justify whether a relationship is multiplicative or additive, and to meet a scaled counter-case, brings the reasoning into the open and can check whether the learner gives the right answer for the right reason.
learnerActions: Face a mentor who presents tables and asks for each: 'is it times, or more than? How do you know?'
Defend your classification by pointing to the constant multiple and showing that the difference changes down the table.
Respond to a scaled counter-case when you give an additive answer — e.g. 'you said +4; check the next row, does +4 still work?'
Explain, before mixing any paint, whether a 2:6 batch will be darker, lighter or the same shade as a 1:3 batch, and why.
activities.title: Justify it: times or more than?
